articles.title: Far from farms and cities, dry climates are boosting river nitrate pollution
articles.author: Li Li (李黎), Professor of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Penn State
paras: Typically, when people hear about nitrates, it involves runoff from farm fields, sewage systems and cities that can fuel harmful algae blooms and raise the risk of a serious illness in infants known as “blue baby syndrome.”

But a river can also run through a sparsely populated landscape with little farming and still contain surprisingly high levels of this form of nitrogen that can harm aquatic life, drinking water and human health.

In a new study, my colleague and I found a reason why that happens: Dry climate conditions are associated with high river nitrate concentrations, even in places with little farming or urban development.

We found nitrate hot spots in some unexpected places, including the Rocky Mountains of the western United States and northern Africa’s Sahara Desert. Where water is scarce, we found that nitrates – which can naturally leach into surface water and groundwater from the soil as microbes break down organic material – were able to accumulate and become concentrated rather than being diluted or flushed away.

That raises health concerns for regions where nitrates in rivers and well water might not be given much thought. It also raises questions about how nitrate-related health risks will increase as global temperatures rise.

To see how widespread this pattern is, we combined global measurements from more than 7,000 monitoring sites and additionally extracted information about climate, soils, land use and other landscape features. We then trained machine learning models to estimate long-term average nitrate concentrations across nearly 2.9 million river segments worldwide.
The resulting map suggests that nitrates deserve attention well beyond the urban and agricultural regions where they are usually monitored.

High nitrate exposure in water and food is particularly dangerous for infants because it can interfere with the blood’s ability to carry oxygen. Blue baby syndrome, or methemoglobinemia, can result in serious illnesses and be caused by nitrate poisoning.
The U.S. drinking water standard of 10 milligrams of nitrate-nitrogen per liter was established primarily to guard against this acute risk.
We estimate that about 37,000 people worldwide live in areas where rivers exceed the 10 mg/L drinking water standard, predominantly in the U.S. Corn Belt.

That doesn’t mean 37,000 people are drinking water at those concentrations, since river water in many regions is treated before it is supplied for drinking. But it’s a concerning level they should be aware of, particularly those using well water.

Research has also raised concerns about possible effects of long-term exposure to nitrate at lower concentrations, including certain cancers and adverse birth outcomes, such as babies born preterm or with a low birth weight, although those risks are still being studied.
We estimate that about 480 million people worldwide live in areas where nearby rivers have elevated long-term average nitrate concentrations, above 2.5 milligrams per liter.

Many of the rivers our models identified as having elevated nitrate levels are small headwater streams. Many headwater streams cease to flow for some periods of time every year, and nitrates can accumulate to high concentrations under dry or low-flow conditions. These small streams make up most of the global river networks, have long been overlooked and feed larger rivers that supply drinking water to large populations and help shape the quality of water downstream.
Too much nitrate in rivers and lakes can also fuel algal growth and disrupt aquatic ecosystems.

A global map of nitrate concentrations in river water cannot show what comes out of someone’s tap. Their water may be mixed with other sources or treated before they drink it. Nitrate concentrations can also rise and fall over time, while our map shows long-term averages.
To understand a person’s actual exposure will require connecting river measurements with drinking water sources, treatment practices and tests of water delivered to households.

Many rivers with nitrate concentrations above 2.5 milligrams per liter flow through sparsely populated regions where access to treated drinking water may be limited. Even where treatment facilities exist, conventional methods remove little nitrate. Removing it requires specialized technologies that can be costly to operate.

Our study shows why more drylands and small headwater streams need to be monitored for nitrate. It also raises a question for a warming world: If a region becomes drier, how much will nitrate concentrations rise even if people do not add more nitrogen to the landscape?

Answering that will require measurements through wet and dry periods, paired with studies of how water moves through soils, groundwater and rivers. For now, the message is clear: Protecting water quality requires paying attention to the climate as well as to the human activities that put nitrogen into the environment.

articles.title: Extreme weather risk is scaring big corporations away from poorer countries – that hurts the companies, too
articles.author: Jonas Gamso, Associate Professor of International Trade and Global Studies, Arizona State University
paras: When multinational companies decide where to build a factory, open a mine or establish a regional office, they have to consider whether the investment will still be profitable years into the future.

Making that decision increasingly means thinking about risks, like whether surrounding roads will flood, worker safety will be compromised by extreme heat in the summer, and clean water will be available.

As climate change increases the frequency and intensity of extreme weather events around the world, these effects can be especially severe in poorer countries that lack the resources to prepare for disasters or recover quickly after they hit.

I study how political and environmental risks affect international business. In my new book, “Multinational Corporations and Climate Change: Risks, Responsibilities, and Resilience,” I explore how disaster risk is affecting the ways global companies see these climate-vulnerable markets, and how those views are leading some foreign investors to avoid these developing nations altogether.

Low- and middle-income countries aren’t the only ones that suffer when multinational corporations pass them by. The companies themselves also stand to lose out on business opportunities in emerging markets if they pull away.
How climate risk affects foreign investment

Evidence from several studies suggests that multinationals are systematically avoiding investing in the most climate-vulnerable countries. These include my own analysis of 159 countries. Although these studies focus on different samples, they identify the same trend: Countries characterized by greater climate vulnerability received less foreign investment.

The results are not trivial. My book identifies a 12% reduction in foreign direct investment for each 1-point rise in climate vulnerability on a 100-point scale, while holding other relevant factors constant. This vulnerability data measures countries’ exposure to climate hazards as well as their capacity to adapt.
Companies rarely say why they’re avoiding a particular location, but their climate-related concerns occasionally become visible.

For example, Google halted plans to build a US$200 million data center in Chile after an environmental court revoked its construction permit over the likely effects on water supplies and the environment. Similarly, a $1 billion data center proposed in Kenya by Microsoft and the Abu Dhabi-based artificial intelligence company G42 was delayed and ultimately suspended amid concerns about water stress in the area.
Companies have reason to be cautious about climate risks.

One analysis of 71 large publicly traded companies found that firms reporting major flood losses experienced a 5% average decline in shareholder value over the following year, after accounting for broader market movements.
In Vietnam, typhoons and floods caused an estimated $475 million in damage to energy and transportation infrastructure in 2022. Unreliable infrastructure cost companies there about $280 million.

Severe flooding in Thailand in 2011 forced several companies, including Toyota, Nissan and Honda, to temporarily suspend production as factories flooded, shutting down production of parts or vehicles made there.
Costs like those shape where companies choose to invest next.

While climate risk does not stop all investment in climate-vulnerable markets, it does make projects in these nations relatively more expensive, less attractive and more difficult to finance than less risky locations.
Who loses from investor avoidance?

For developing countries, less foreign investment means fewer jobs are created. These countries also have fewer opportunities to benefit from exposure to the new technologies that multinationals bring when they invest abroad.

Those results highlight another way climate change is deepening global inequality. It reduces the economic activity that could support future development, while simultaneously damaging physical infrastructure and threatening human health and well-being.

Developing countries are especially vulnerable to the effects of rising global temperatures, whether for their dependence on agricultural markets, geography or relatively fragile infrastructure. A report from the Climate Impact Lab at the University of Chicago projects that 90% of heat-related deaths in the coming decades will take place in low- and middle-income countries. Similarly, a 2022 study found that around 90% of people exposed to flooding live in developing nations.

Yet poor countries have contributed only a tiny fraction of the emissions that are causing climate change, even as they face the brunt of the damage. For example, African countries are responsible for less than 4% of greenhouse gas emissions globally. But they stand to experience the greatest negative effects of climate change.
Lost opportunities for multinational companies
When a company avoids investing in climate-vulnerable countries, that may reduce its exposure to floods, droughts or extreme heat, but the decision also carries potential costs for the company.

Many of these countries have growing consumer markets, energy resources or critical minerals that multinationals need. Companies that dismiss them as too risky may lose out on promising opportunities.

For example, the Democratic Republic of Congo supplies most of the world’s cobalt, while Indonesia has become the dominant producer of nickel. These countries are highly vulnerable to climate change, which is likely scaring some companies away.

Yet companies with a greater tolerance for risk have established strong positions in those countries’ mineral industries. Thus, more cautious firms may reduce their risk exposure, but they are also surrendering access to important resources and growing markets.
Reducing investor avoidance
There are ways to help companies overcome their climate-risk avoidance so more investment can pour into these countries:

Foreign aid from wealthy countries can help developing countries shore up their roads, ports, electrical grids and water systems before extreme storms or droughts occur. My 2025 study found that climate-vulnerable countries that received more aid for climate adaptation also received more foreign direct investment than those receiving less aid. The result suggests the funding may reassure companies that climate risks are being addressed.

International development banks can share some of the risks by providing climate risk insurance to multinationals. This would offer a safety net to absorb some of the losses if a covered disruption prevents a project from operating as intended. The World Bank already offers similar coverage against political risk incidents, which has given companies confidence to invest in countries such as Kenya, Mozambique and Nigeria.

Better data can give companies more precise information about climate risks. Many risk scores label entire nations as vulnerable or not, even though exposure varies from one city or project site to another. More detailed information about local flood exposure, water availability, heat, infrastructure and adaptation capabilities would allow companies to limit their avoidance to the riskiest areas, instead of bypassing those countries altogether.

Understanding the local risk, insuring companies against risk and helping countries make their infrastructure more resilient to storms, droughts and heat can help boost investment in ways that benefit the companies and spur economic growth and development in climate-vulnerable countries at the same time.

articles.title: El Niño threatens health, too – early warnings done right can save lives
articles.author: Kimberley Miner, Research Professor in Earth Sciences, University of Maine
paras: As communities around the world shore up their infrastructure in anticipation of one of the most powerful El Niños on record in late 2026 and early 2027, they need to think about rising health risks, too – and include them in early weather warnings.

El Niño is part of a natural climate phenomenon that shifts global weather patterns for months at a time. During El Niño years, global temperatures tend to rise, triggering heat waves; normally dry regions can be hit with flooding rainfall; and normally wet regions often face droughts. All carry serious health risks.

In southern Africa, for example, forecasters are warning of a rising risk of severe drought that could affect the 2026-27 growing season in key farming regions. At the same time, wetter-than-normal conditions in the Horn of Africa raise the risk of flooding and mosquito-borne disease outbreaks there.

Dry conditions in Southeast Asia are already fueling wildfires and sending water supplies falling. October downpours in Chile triggered mudslides that left a mess for people to clean up in homes and yards.
In the United States, the South tends to be wetter than normal during El Niño years; drought is more likely in the Northern Plains; and storms can be fierce, particularly along the Pacific Coast.
As researchers in psychology, global health and Earth system science, we study how environmental disruptions affect people’s health and their ability to respond.
To protect the population, communities need plans that keep care accessible and weather warnings that provide advice people can act on before, during and after a disaster.
When extreme weather becomes a health emergency
The health consequences of extreme weather events often extend beyond the immediate hazard.
For example, research has linked exposure to flooding, wildfire and ecosystem changes with elevated risks of illnesses, psychological distress and chronic stress.

Floodwater can lead to infections, such as hepatitis, cryptosporidium and fungal diseases, as well as longer-term health damage through exposure to harmful environmental microbes, chemicals and an increase in disease-carrying vectors such as mosquitoes.
Drought can lead to poor air quality and, in some places, malnutrition.
Disasters can also keep people from getting essential healthcare, disrupt their livelihoods and displace them from their homes and social networks.

The threat of a changing, potentially unsafe environment can also increase anticipatory, long-term distress. The World Health Organization identifies anxiety and post-traumatic stress as mental health consequences of extreme weather-related hazards. We believe mental health counseling services also belong in communities’ preparedness and recovery plans, not as an optional add-on after addressing physical needs.
Vulnerable populations face even higher risks

For people with existing illnesses or in areas far from medical care, extreme weather brings additional risks. These individuals and healthcare systems benefit from early warnings about El Niño’s disaster risks that help them prepare well in advance.

At least 2.5 million Americans rely on in-home electricity-powered medical equipment, such as oxygen concentrators and ventilators, including nearly 78,000 who receive dialysis at home to help their kidneys function. When the power goes out or water is disrupted, they risk losing use of what may be life-sustaining equipment.

Distance compounds these risks. Many communities around the world don’t have local clinics. Rural Americans live an average of 10.5 miles (17 kilometers) from the nearest hospital, and for 1 in 4 rural residents, the trip takes more than 30 minutes on average – before a single road floods. During Hurricane Harvey in 2017, flooding limited access to Houston’s second-busiest hospital for five days. The most extensive disruptions were in lower-income and minority neighborhoods.

With advanced warnings, community organizations and healthcare providers preparing for El Niño can contact people with health vulnerabilities early to arrange backup power supplies and help them prepare so they know what to do when disasters do strike.
How to turn forecasts into protection
A good weather warning doesn’t just name the threat. It also provides information that residents can act on to stay safe through the disaster and the recovery afterward.

Communities do not need to wait until a disaster is building to begin preparing. Existing community emergency plans, patient outreach programs and social networks provide a starting point for steps that help.
First, communities can identify where disruptions could become public health emergencies.

State departments of health and other social services can combine regional weather outlooks with local information about areas facing the highest risks, including the health impacts of water exposure on homes, guidance for avoiding polluted floodwaters and evacuation routes.
Community organizations can help identify individuals and neighborhoods that may face language barriers and ensure they receive lifesaving alerts and information they can understand.
Second, it’s important to protect continuity of clinical care for patients during disasters.

Health systems and public health departments can coordinate with health providers in hospitals, pharmacies and home health services to identify people who depend on regular medical appointments or transportation and ensure they can still receive care.
In practice, this may be providing flexible scheduling options, organizing alternative means of transportation or identifying alternative care locations that may be more accessible.
Third, weather warnings can be most useful when they provide information people can act on, such as where to find food, transportation or mental health support.

Many local and state emergency services already work to educate the public about storm risks ahead. They can do more by also telling residents where they can find safe water and food, how to limit exposure to chemicals or disease vectors, how to store medicine safely, and whom to contact for transportation, shelter or mental health support.
Information that is specific enough to use and relevant to the community can save lives.
Preparation is preventive care

Because signs of the coming weather shift can be detected months in advance, El Niño forecasts offer something that immediate storm forecasts can’t: extra time to identify these health risks, secure medical care for the months ahead and prepare so warnings are useful to residents.
When warnings pair information about the risk with practical actions and local resources, they can empower people rather than leaving them feeling helpless in the face of a disaster.

articles.title: The SS United States has been deliberately sunk – this is how marine life will colonise the world’s largest artificial reef
articles.author: Nicholas Ray, Doctoral Programmes Manager and Researcher in Aquatic Ecology, Nottingham Trent University
paras: As a marine ecologist and keen scuba diver, I’ve long been fascinated by what happens when a large structure is introduced to the sea. Within hours, microscopic organisms begin colonising its surfaces, forming a thin biological layer. Over the following months and years, barnacles, mussels, sponges and other marine life become established, creating a new habitat that attracts fish and a diverse range of species.

This week, one of the world’s most famous ocean liners, the SS United States, was sunk off the coast of Florida. At 302 metres long, it has become the world’s largest artificial reef. It is a very exciting prospect to one day dive on such a giant, and to see how it changes as marine life makes it home.

The SS United States was built as a luxury ocean liner, and its maiden voyage in 1952 captured the coveted Blue Riband by crossing the Atlantic in only three days and ten hours – a passenger liner record that remains unbroken.

As the years went by, commercial jetliners superseded transatlantic sea travel, and the vessel was retired and neglected for decades. Rather than facing the ignominy of a breaker’s yard, the legendary ship was bought by Okaloosa County, Florida, to turn it into a diving attraction.

The SS United States is a particularly enormous structure to introduce to the seabed – longer even than the Titanic. It will rest in around 55 metres of water, with its upper sections rising to within about 17 metres of the surface. This will create habitats at different depths, making it an unusually varied site for both wildlife and divers of different abilities.
It will also eclipse the nearby 275-metre aircraft carrier USS Oriskany, deliberately sunk in 2006, to become the largest artificial reef on Earth.
So what do we expect to happen? Here’s a suggested ecological succession pattern, month-by-month.
First, microorganisms arrive

The first organisms to colonise the SS United States will be almost invisible. Within hours of immersion, marine bacteria and microalgae will begin attaching themselves to its cleaned metal surfaces, forming a thin layer of “biofilm”.

This slime is the foundation of the new ecosystem. As the biofilm develops, it releases chemical cues that help drifting larvae recognise the surface as a suitable place to settle. Carried by Gulf currents, these tiny organisms begin attaching themselves to the structure. By the end of the first three months, a variety of small animals and algae will have established themselves on the hull, beginning the transformation of bare metal into a living reef.
Then the ship becomes covered in marine life

As the biofilm matures, larger organisms arrive to feed on it. These include more mobile invertebrates like sea urchins and porcelain crabs, and filter-feeders like oysters and mussels which attach themselves to vertical walls where the currents tend to send the most nutrients their way.
Fish and larger predators move in

By the end of the first year, hard corals will begin to establish themselves permanently. The transformation will still be in its early stages, but over the next five to ten years the hull will become increasingly encrusted with corals, sponges and other marine life. At some point, casual divers will no longer see a ship covered in coral, but a coral-covered reef that happens to contain a ship.
As the reef develops, fish will be attracted by the shelter and the growing supply of food. Smaller fish will begin to find refuge to evade open-water predators.

Snappers and groupers are among the medium-sized reef fish that will begin to take up permanent residency around the wreck, using the long internal corridors for protection. Larger predators, including barracuda, king mackerel and sharks, could also patrol its decks and upper sections.

The ship’s enormous size and varied structure will offer a range of habitats, from sheltered spaces for smaller fish to exposed areas where larger, free-swimming species can hunt. Over time, these interactions could create a complex food web, turning the wreck into a significant biological hotspot.

A common misconception is that artificial reefs simply concentrate fish that were already present, leaving surrounding waters poorer. In reality, while some fish are attracted from elsewhere, a large reef structure also creates vast amounts of new habitat and food.

As corals, sponges, barnacles and other reef builders colonise the wreck, they create food and shelter that did not previously exist, allowing the ecosystem to support more life overall. The result is generally not an underwater crowd gathered around a ship, but a gradual increase in the total amount of marine life the area can support.

Another widespread misconception is that marine scientists “seed” artificial reefs with organisms or their larvae. In reality, colonisation happens naturally: the Gulf of Mexico already harbours an abundant pool of drifting larvae and migratory fish. Artificially introducing marine life is unnecessary and risks introducing non-native species or pathogens.

Instead, human engineering is largely about preparing the ship for sinking. This includes removing hazards such as oil, asbestos and loose wires, and sealing off parts of the vessel to prevent divers getting disorientated or lost in silt-outs deep in the hull.

The scuttling of the SS United States represents a rare convergence of maritime history, ecology, and engineering. Transformed into the world’s largest artificial reef, this record-breaking ocean liner could potentially anchor a vibrant marine ecosystem for decades to come. I’m looking forward to seeing how that transformation unfolds – and maybe, one day, exploring it myself.

articles.title: UK appoints new climate security envoy – here’s what she could change
articles.author: James Dyke, Assistant Director of the Global Systems Institute, University of Exeter
paras: The UK government has just appointed Madeleine Alessandri as the world’s first special representative for climate security.

Prime minister Andy Burnham announced the new role in his speech at the UN climate summit, Cop31, in Turkey. This, he said, would be part of “a new era of British leadership on climate”. He also cited climate as “a national security issue” – a sign that Burnham considers this environmental crisis a significant risk to the country’s social stability and economy.
With a remit to “support ministers to champion UK leadership on climate and nature security”, Alessandri will report to the foreign secretary.

Climate change has long been considered as a threat multiplier because it compounds and increases many risks to national security. Unfortunately, many governments have failed to acknowledge such threats, resulting in a dangerous blind spot.

For example, a warmer world will produce more erratic weather that will impact harvests. Less food produces price spikes. In order to try to ensure food security, governments implement export controls. This can cause globally traded food prices to spike driving people into food poverty, exacerbate tensions and lead to conflict.
The 2026 UK harvest is the worst on record. Four of the five worst harvests have happened since 2020. This puts further pressure on UK farmers.

As climate security envoy, one of Alessandri’s priorities will need to be the state of national food security. That’s because the UK imports 40% of the food it consumes and so is extremely exposed to the tightening of global food supply.

Given that this year’s super El Niño (when certain parts of the Pacific are warmer than usual) is already creating havoc around the world, Alessandri may soon find herself embroiled in efforts to ensure that the responses to the consequences of the climate crisis do not make the situation worse.

Responding to extreme weather and climate consequences can produce derailment risks whereby efforts to reduce climate change get blown off course by escalating climate and social destabilisation. For example, in response to rising food insecurity national governments can ban food exports. This increases food prices even further. Protests over the cost of living can spiral into wider unrest. All this can make it difficult to maintain the political will required to progress the energy transition.

Alessandri is a career civil servant and the former chair of the UK’s joint intelligence committee (JIC) which oversees the UK’s secret intelligence services. Until now, the security implications of climate change sat within Katie White’s remit as the UK’s minister for climate transition in the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero.

It is perhaps no coincidence that it was the JIC that commissioned the previously supressed report on the national security implications of climate change. While published by the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs, it is widely acknowledged that the national security assessment on global ecosystems was produced by the JIC while Allesandri was leading it.

She will now be in a position to negotiate directly with other nations and organisations specifically about the food and wider security impacts of climate change. I would expect other governments to create similar roles in the near future because climate change is rapidly rising up the ranks of issues that are relevant to national security.

articles.title: Climate change has different consequences for the health of women and men – but the systems tracking it don’t reflect that
articles.author: Kent Buse, Professor of Health Policy, Director of Programme Development, Monash University Malaysia, Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, Monash University; Imperial College London
paras: The health risks men and women are exposed to and the illnesses they develop vary widely across lifetimes and places. Yet climate policy and health services often overlook these differences.

Some of these differences are stark. For example, more women than men die from being exposed to the smoke of cooking fires, but for most of adult life a man is more likely to die from this exposure than a woman of the same age. In Europe, studies of individual heatwaves have found women to be at higher risk of heat-related death.

In Latin America and the Caribbean though, men die from heat-related causes at nearly twice the rate that women do, according to the Global Burden of Disease study. Coordinated by the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation, this study is the largest systematic effort ever made to count what kills people and what makes them ill, producing comparable estimates of deaths, disease and disability for every country, by age and sex, every year since 1990.

Despite these inequities, the monitoring systems that track climate change and its effects on health fail to capture the full picture. Much of the data is categorised by gender when collected, but when the data is transferred to the monitoring systems, the experiences of women and men are merged into a single total. As a result, the decision-making that informs climate policy and health systems is underpinned by data that is oversimplified.

We have just audited four of those systems: the Belém Adaptation Indicators agreed at last year’s UN climate summit in Brazil, the World Health Organization’s survey of health ministries, a scorecard that grades countries’ climate plans on health and the Lancet Countdown, an annual scientific stock take. Of the 45 indicators from across these four reports that measure people’s lives (rather than tracking systems or plans), only one reports results separately for women and men.

All four reports draw on surveys and death registers that are often separated by sex, then published as one merged figure. That total is what reaches the people who decide what counts as progress and where the money goes.

That might be a philanthropic funder choosing which programmes to back, a government filling in the UN’s new adaptation scorecard in the only format its definitions allow, or the negotiators who will use those scorecards to judge whether the world is adapting in 2028 at Cop33.
At the UN climate summit Cop31, currently underway in Antalya, Turkey, we have an opportunity to change what gets reported in the future about how climate affects men and women’s health.

Sex and gender shape climate risk. Data is often reported by sex but then differences are explained by a combination of sex and gender (social roles, norms, structures). The biological makeup of human bodies affects how they physiologically respond differently to heat and smoke. Pregnancy brings additional risks.
The gendered norms of daily life put women and men in different places and situations: who works on a building site in 40°C heat, who cooks indoors over wood, who can get to a clinic.
It is easy to assume that women bear the greater risk. Often they do, but only accurately categorised data can tell us if that is always the case.

Women are more exposed to smoke from cooking stoves, for example, and it claims a larger share of their overall ill health, yet it kills more men. This is because men often reach midlife with hearts and lungs already damaged by a range of factors such as smoking and by the dust, fumes and diesel exhaust of working in mines, on building sites, farms and near traffic, so a smaller exposure to cooking smoke does greater damage.

The point is not to pit the sexes against each other. Knowing why they differ, whether through exposure, susceptibility or access to cooling, transport or care, tells you where to intervene. A single total hides all of that nuance.

We assessed a total of 211 indicators based on whether they reveal whether women and men are affected differently. Only the Lancet Countdown’s count of outdoor workers does. Of the 166 indicators that measure plans, systems and environments, only five mention sex or gender in some way.
A publishing decision, not a data gap

For much of this gap, the data already exists. The Lancet Countdown’s own methods appendix shows that three of its indicators use data split by sex and then merge it before publication. The Belém indicators that count people will draw on household surveys, death registers and workforce records, which routinely report by sex. These could be published by sex in the next reporting cycle with little or no new data collection.
Where the data is really missing or scattered, filling the gap costs money, and that is where climate and health funders could make the most difference.
The Belém indicators are the UN’s new yardstick for whether countries are adapting to climate change, but the details of each indicator remain to be written.

Decisions still need to be made at the global level on what each indicator measures, which data sources they use, and whether results are broken down by groups such as women and men. These detailed definitions, the output of a technical working group, are due to be agreed in November 2027.

Countries will then build their reporting systems around them. The record so far is not encouraging. Of the 16 expert proposals for health indicators circulated in May 2025, three asked for results by sex. By September 2025 there was one. The eight adopted at Cop30 in November 2025 include none.

The technical group was due to be formed in June 2026, but governments could not agree who should sit on it, so the decision returns to Cop31. If it includes people who know how to produce statistics by sex, and if reporting by sex becomes the default wherever the source data already have it, the next decade of climate adaptation can show who it reached – and who is being left behind.

We will repeat our audit as each framework updates. This means that governments will know whether their adaptation is reaching men and women equitably according to need. Funders will know whether their money is.

Kent Buse is Co-CEO of Global 50/50 whose report is mentioned in this piece. He is also an unpaid board member and trustee of the World Obesity Federation. Global 50/50 is funded by the Gates Foundation.

articles.title: BBC documentary takes eight children on a nature field trip to explore eco-anxiety
articles.author: Michael Joseph Richardson, Senior Lecturer in Human Geography, Newcastle University
paras: A dawn chorus begins with the chirping and tweeting of birds, wind blowing through the trees and a woodpecker hammering on wood. Dappled sunlight bursts through the forest canopy, and an evocative choir of children join the birds in song:

We will stand up tall in the shadow of your power. For every empty promise, we will shout it even louder. No more sacrifice or compromise for profits, greed and lies. It’s time to build the future; Don’t ignore the children’s cries.

This powerful opening to Climate Change and Me: Future Council, an environmental documentary currently showing on the BBC, quickly shifts to a lighter tone. After running over mossy undergrowth through the forest, the children respond cheekily to the director’s call for another take.

Play can open up different learning and communication styles, particularly for younger children. This is something Australian director Damon Gameau taps into throughout the one-hour programme as he leads a fieldtrip around Europe. Eight climate-conscious children, selected from over 1,000 applicants aged nine to 16, travel together on the “Bumblebus” – a yellow American-style schoolbus, powered by biofuel – in pursuit of a brighter, greener future.

Aspects of this programme remind me of my own research. I work as a storyteller on a project called Birds, Bees, Bikes and Trees. Our team’s work is wide-ranging. Over the past three years, I have worked with a group of 20 young fathers to explore the everyday environmental actions they can (and often do) take. I have also led sessions in classrooms exploring urban relationships to nature through science and storytelling with more than 300 schoolchildren. Our design of these activities is shaped by care and curiosity, not anger or anxiety.

I am drawn particularly to the BBC programme’s use of magical realism. This artistic style of storytelling is similar to a novum within science fiction – a literary device such as time travel that distorts reality. In making both the familiar strange and the mythical mundane, it can open our imagination to new possibilities. I use this approach in my own work.

Don’t Look Down, for example is an upcoming children’s storybook I have created with primary schoolchildren in Newcastle and with Atomhawk, a video game art studio. Their illustrations convey an imaginary world abandoned by adults in a relentless pursuit of growth and innovation. Through this alternative future, a child can begin to ask questions of the world in which they live, and the stories they have been told about how to care for it.

Back to the TV screen, and Gameau’s show features several scenes where some of the eight children are led to tears. There is sadness, anger and frustration. Some say they feel overwhelmed by pressure to make the planet a better place and fix a world which they did not break.

By Lake Geneva, the children meet with climate activist Clover Hogan to offload some of their strong feelings. Hogan is also an eco-anxiety researcher. In 2019, she founded a youth-driven not-for-profit organisation called Force of Nature which brings young people into conversations with decision-makers. She explains to the children that their anxiety is a healthy response and shows that they care. Hogan says: “When we feel that sadness, when we feel that anger, when we feel that frustration, that is the internal alarm bell that tells us something is really, really wrong.”
The show advocates for involving children and young people in decision-making. This is both an admirable and achievable mission.

At the Nestlé corporation headquarters in Switzerland, the children meet with the global head of public affairs for this food and drink multinational. They press him hard on Nestlé’s lack of climate action and on the firm’s excessive use of single-use plastic packaging. They called out “empty words and empty promises” and one challenged him with damning words: “You are not a powerful leader, you are a disgrace.”

The film depicts the children’s anger as righteous. There is evidence to suggest that eco-anger is a more productive emotion than eco-anxiety. But there is a risk that young’s people activism plays into the trope of powerful elites, if too narrowly defined by either anxiety or anger.

While both are key features of this programme, recent research identifies a wider range of responses to climate change. In doing so, the researchers encourage expanding our vocabulary on climate change and how we experience it, to avoid overly reductive responses to this environmental crisis.

Informed by my own research, I had hoped to see more reflection on the transformative potential of nature for mental health benefits. Children should not be defined as being without hope, power or influence but nor should nature.

Young people can claim their agency and be encouraged to actively build their green future, as my project will be doing at a green jobs career event for young people. That green future could involve the representation of younger generations on the boards of big companies, but it might also involve community power or nature-positive regeneration projects. The choice could be theirs.
Michael Joseph Richardson has received funding from the National Lottery Community Fund and the Economic and Social Research Council Impact Accelerator Account.

articles.title: Democrats are at Cop31 to show that the US has not abandoned the fight against climate change
articles.author: Natasha Lindstaedt, Professor in the Department of Government, University of Essex
paras: The results of the US midterms on November 3 delivered a resounding victory for the Democrats, and a major loss for US president Donald Trump and the Republican party.

Gaining control of the Senate and the House of Representatives has emboldened the Democrats, giving them a renewed sense of political legitimacy and a mandate to pursue their agenda. But will this shift translate into meaningful changes in US climate change policy?

The Democratic sweep will change the political dynamics around US climate policy and how the country cooperates with the international community on this issue. Although there was no official US presence at the 2025 Cop conference, held in Brazil, a coalition of 100 local US leaders, including governors, mayors and other top city and state officials, attended as part of the US Climate Alliance. Former US vice-president Al Gore, and former US secretary of state John Kerry are part of an unofficial US group at the 2026 gathering.
Kerry said in a speech there: “Americans are committed to taking back their future, and we will build and rebuild our partnerships as we do that.”

Being on the ground at Cop is important. As the US has a decisive role to play in global climate policy, sending a non-official coalition signals that many Americans are still working to combat climate change.

Trump has repeatedly stated that climate change is a hoax and refused to attend the Cop31 climate talks being held in Turkey. But 20 Democratic members of Congress will be attending, although they have been denied official state department funding for the trip.

During the first and second Trump administrations, the US has been an outlier among wealthy countries when it comes to fighting climate change. Trump has actively backed the use of fossil fuels, undermining clean energy projects, and rolled back legislation that stipulated emission standards for vehicles.

Trump also weakened greenhouse gas reporting requirements and methane regulation. Then in February 2026, the Trump administration rescinded the Environmental Protection Agency’s 2009 finding that greenhouse gases threaten the health and welfare of the public, which had regulated the emissions from new cars and other vehicles. This had provided the legal foundation for regulation under the Clean Air Act.

On the international front, Trump was equally determined to undermine global efforts to fight climate change. Famously, he withdrew from the Paris agreement, part of a global initiative to address climate change, and refused to attend Cop summits. But the Democrats’ seismic midterm win may be a sign of optimism for those fighting to address climate change.
Data centres are big issue

The biggest issues of the midterms were affordability, corruption and the Iran war, but issues related to fighting climate change were also on voters’ list. There is growing concern about data centres. As many as 56% of US voters felt that data centres and AI were either a major or even crucial factor in influencing who they voted for, with only 13% saying it was not a factor at all.

Data centres require millions of gallons of water for cooling systems, and this is expected to rise to 73 billion litres of water a year by 2028. Over half of planned AI facilities in the US will be situated in areas that have significant water shortages or drought conditions.

After the midterms, Zoe Lofgren, a Democrat, is likely to become the chair of the House of Representatives’ committee on science, space and technology once the new session starts in January. She wants to tackle the administration’s “climate denialism”.
Lofgren’s leadership, along with new Democratic members of the committee, may offer it more power to reverse some of the Trump administration’s changes to science policy.

However, the Democrat midterm wins will not mean that the US is automatically back at the negotiating table at Cop nor that the US will be able to rejoin the Paris Accords while Trump is president. Trump still has the power to make these decisions and can continue to keep the US out of international climate initiatives, regardless of who controls Congress. The US Constitution says nothing about withdrawing from treaties, which creates uncertainty for what the Senate’s role might be.

The election, however, does signal that there is considerable domestic opposition to his approach. And while Congress has not passed follow-up legislation prohibiting presidential withdrawal from the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), it has continued to fund several UNFCCC initiatives. During the Biden administration, the US significantly increased climate finance from US$1.5 billion (£1.1 billion) a year in 2021 to US$9.5 billion in 2023.

Democrats could also push back on Trump’s current policies, using their power to hold hearings, investigate the administration’s dismantling of climate programmes and challenge cuts to scientific research. The Democrats can also use the power of Congress’s control of spending to protect or restore funding to some of these environmental initiatives.

They could also try to introduce legislation that reinstates some of the clean energy initiatives that had been implemented in past administrations to strengthen emissions standards and support clean energy. The big issue, however, is that Trump has made it clear that he is going to be very active in using his veto power, and without a two-thirds majority in Congress, the Democrats will not be able to override this.
What does this mean globally?

What this all means is that the world cannot expect the US to be a reliable and constructive partner at Cop with Trump still in power. Trump will probably continue to forge ahead with expanding fossil fuel production, while weakening international climate cooperation, even if the electorate disapproves of these policies.

Ironically, Trump’s greatest contribution to the fight against climate change was his initiation of the war with Iran, which helped to cut global fossil fuel carbon dioxide emissions by 0.4% due the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. But climate scientists note this is not a long-term solution.

While the Democrats’ electoral victory offers a glimmer of hope for renewed climate action, both domestically and internationally, restoring US climate leadership will take time, especially while Trump remains in power.

articles.title: Transforming climate policy into creative writing: an alternative way to experience UN summits
articles.author: Bernadette McBride, Lecturer in Creative Writing, Liverpool Hope University
paras: Formal agendas of climate summits can provide a rich source of material for creative writers. The craft of imaginative storytelling can help cut through jargon and render the ecological stakes more immediate, relatable and urgently felt.

Every year, I facilitate an intensive university course on reimagining climate futures through eco-focused creative writing. In 2024, that short course coincided with the UN climate summit, Cop29 in Baku, Azerbaijan. That was a controversial choice for climate talks, as the host nation stated it intended to expand its gas production by up to a third over the subsequent decade.
The goals of my creative writing workshop were to write with climate realism in mind, deliberately steering clear of worn, apocalyptic, end-of-the-world tropes.

The group was varied, ranging from younger undergraduates interested in climate activism to seasoned eco-poets and students from unrelated disciplines such as natural sciences. To ground our discussions in live events, I used several breaking news reports concerning Cop29 alongside extracts from official agendas documents and programme overviews as prompts for creative writing.

I was genuinely struck by how riled the students became when responding to the commitments outlined in Cop29 and broader international environmental policy. The participants were deeply critical of these promises. The interesting thing was how this fuelled and filled the room with lively, topical discussions, driving them to produce creative work that pushed boundaries.

The second part of the course coincided with a severe weather warning labelled a “danger to life” by the Met Office. We sat and watched streetlights swaying dangerously outside the classroom window in Liverpool as Storm Bert battered the country in late November 2024.

Just a week earlier, I had shared a UK government emergency preparedness brief as another writing stimulus. We had read the short story Outage by fiction writer Ian Critchley, about an older couple facing disability and struggling to cope in a power cut. I asked students to imagine a character forced to navigate that exact official guidance amid an unfolding crisis.

As a point of reference, we examined Megan Hunter’s novel-turned-film The End We Start From, starring Jodie Comer. The narrative follows a heavily pregnant protagonist, in labour and frantically calling emergency services as her London home fills with water – but, because of the widespread flooding, she finds there is no assistance. Those scenes highlight the worrying limitations of standard advice to simply “call for help” during the world catastrophes that Cop summits seek to address.
When the hypothetical scenarios we had all imagined and creatively written about became part of reality as Storm Bert hit, it felt like an eerie wake-up call.

Policy jargon, though often dense and alienating, can serve as an effective springboard for discussing difficult realities. It can give writers an accessible entry point, and a climate summit can provide a tangible event to focus on. The official Cop29 agenda, along with local council contingency policies, directly inspired more than ten distinctive poems and short stories.

The emotions evoked by these policy frameworks are more than enough to encourage creative writing that capture both the fragile hopes and real fears bound up with our climate present and future. While decision-makers may not always prove reliable narrators of our shared future, the institutional platforms they command do provide raw material for those of us who want to tell the true human and more-than-human stories.

Global summits can provoke a radical reimagining of ecological futures. As Cop31 takes place this month in Antalya, Turkey, the world public must examine these official pledges, especially those that falter or remain unfulfilled. These contested spaces represent the very realities writers must capture and hold at the front of their minds.

As the author Amitav Ghosh has questioned in his 2016 book The Great Derangement: Climate Change and the Unthinkable, where is the serious fiction about climate change? Writing through a postcolonial lens, Ghosh highlights that contemporary literature still suffers from a shortage of narratives addressing environmental crises beyond the dominant western perspective.

Because UN climate summits bring together delegations from across the globe, they offer vital opportunities to register and articulate multiple perspectives from frontline populations, from low-lying small island developing states to large industrial nations.

articles.title: COP31: Governments are failing to rein in emissions from their own power plants
articles.author: Don Grant, Professor of Sociology, University of Colorado Boulder
paras: World leaders meeting at the annual U.N. climate summit in November 2026 are wrestling with a persistent challenge: how to get countries to follow through on their commitments to reduce greenhouse gas emissions that are warming the planet.

One of the biggest problems has long been fossil fuel power plants, but new research shows that one type of power plant in particular has been slowest to change: those owned by the very governments making the promises and writing the laws.

My colleagues and I examined carbon dioxide emissions from thousands of fossil-fueled power plants across 134 countries. What we found reveals an important hurdle to achieving the world’s goals for keeping climate change in check.

Although countries have adopted a variety of pricing, regulatory and subsidy measures designed to curb the emissions of the electricity sector, the effectiveness of these climate policies depends on utilities responding to them.

We found that power plants owned by governments had the highest emissions as a group and didn’t cut their emissions as quickly as investor-owned facilities did in response to most policies. That does not necessarily mean they are violating policy requirements, but they were slower to move.
This matters because governments control nearly two-thirds of the world’s electricity-generating capacity.

The results suggest that to limit global warming, governments need to do more than just enact climate policies – they need to ensure that all plants translate those policies into meaningful emissions cuts.
Who owns the plants matters for climate policy
Of the 13,661 power plants that my colleagues Minh Anh Ly and Musabber Ali Chisty and I studied, 5,149 were government-owned – about 38% of them.

But those government-owned plants were responsible for 69% of the carbon emissions, based on the plants we reviewed. Together, power plants are the largest source of climate-warming carbon pollution globally.

On average, we found that government-owned power plants emitted roughly 910,000 metric tons of carbon dioxide annually – three times the average of 290,000 tons for investor-owned plants and over eight times the average of 109,000 for cooperatively owned plants.
Part of the reason for the difference is that governments often invest in large power plants that burn the dirtiest fuel – coal.

However, we also compared the plants’ emissions in 2018 to their emissions a decade earlier and looked at different national policies that were applied over that time. We found some interesting results.
Several policies were statistically associated with investor-owned power plants cutting their emissions from 2009 to 2018, including:
Pricing policies such as carbon taxes that charge companies for emissions released and emission trading systems that set limits that tighten over time.
Fossil fuel subsidy reforms that cut federal support for using fossil fuels.
Regulation policies like air pollution standards and banning and phasing out coal plants.
Renewable portfolio standards that require utilities to expand their use of renewable energy.
Subsidy policies that increase renewable energy use.
But when it came to government-owned power plants, only renewable portfolio standards were associated with significant emissions cuts. The other policies had little effect on their emissions.
These differences also appeared when we examined the stringency of policies, meaning how demanding the policy is, and the amount of time utilities have had to adjust to the policies.
Why governments struggle to clean up
So, what might explain why government-owned utilities respond differently?

Government ownership creates competing pressures that other plants are less subject to. For example, state-owned utilities may be expected to provide affordable electricity, support job growth and generate tax revenue for governments. In countries dependent on payments from companies that extract fossil fuels, utilities may also face political pressure to keep coal and gas facilities operating.

South Africa’s state-owned utility, Eskom, is a prime example. It runs a fleet of aging coal-fired power plants that make it the country’s biggest polluter. But it also provides about 90% of South Africa’s power, and when the country has faced power shortages, it has at times violated emissions standards. Despite years of climate talks, Eskom’s emissions fell little in the 2010s. They have fallen about 16% since 2019, in part due to power outages and more people relying on home solar.

The extra pressure may make it harder for government-owned power plants to reduce their emissions than for private utilities that are accountable to fewer stakeholders and can respond more directly to financial incentives to shift toward cleaner production.

There is also a potential conflict when the same government both regulates and owns a utility. Officials may be reluctant to impose costs that could raise electricity prices or require public subsidies. Our study did not measure enforcement, so we couldn’t establish that publicly owned facilities receive special treatment or disregard legal requirements.
What world leaders can do differently

Our findings suggest that in addition to persuading governments to adopt and enforce more ambitious climate policies, negotiators at the U.N. climate talks will need to get governments to ensure that the power plants they own actually respond to those policies.
Here are three ways governments could do more to get their own power plants to cut emissions.

Governments could follow the example of Ireland and establish emissions-reductions targets specifically for publicly owned utilities and tie managers’ performance reviews, investment approvals and public reporting to measurable progress. Targets are more likely to get attention when managers are held accountable for meeting them. Ireland’s emissions from electricity production fell by more than a quarter from 2019, when it added emissions-reduction targets, to 2025.

They could also do more to address the financial and political constraints their utilities face. In Morocco, for example, international financing helped a state-owned agency expand solar power while limiting costs to electricity consumers. Similar measures, combined with assistance for communities affected by coal-plant closures, could make emissions reductions more feasible.

And governments could pay closer attention to emissions of individual plants as opposed to power sectors as a whole. Publishing comparable annual plant-level emissions and flagging facilities with persistently high pollution would reveal whether sector-wide gains are masking a lack of progress at specific plants.

None of this is to suggest that privatization is the answer to climate change. Government-owned power plants offer special advantages, like coordinating long-term investment and providing reliable electricity in underserved areas. The data shows, however, that for governments to meet their obligations, they need to look closely at their own plants’ emissions, as well.
Don Grant received funding from the National Science Foundation (award # 1824106).

articles.title: Turkey hosts UN climate summit while pursuing new fossil fuel projects
articles.author: Ezgi Unsal, Lecturer in Development Economics, SOAS, University of London
paras: Turkey is making electrification a central theme of this year’s UN climate summit, Cop31, which it is currently hosting in the Mediterranean city of Antalya alongside Australia. The ambition is to raise the share of global energy demand met by electricity from 20% today to 35% by 2035.

But there is a tension in this agenda. More electrification will only cut emissions if the electricity comes from cleaner sources. In Turkey, coal and natural gas still account for more than half of electricity generation, while the country is also pursuing new oil and gas exploration deals. Ahead of a speech at the summit, the country’s president Recep Tayyip Erdoğan announced what he called the “encouraging” discovery of two new oilfields.

Turkey occupies an unusual position under the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), the overall treaty under which the annual climate summits and the Paris agreement emissions targets operate. When the convention was established in 1992, it divided countries into three main groups according to their economic circumstances and responsibilities for tackling climate change.

Annex I countries include industrialised nations and economies in transition that are expected to take the lead in cutting emissions. Annex II is a smaller group of wealthy industrialised nations also required to provide financial and technological support to developing countries. Most developing countries fall outside these annexes and are classified as Non-Annex I.

Turkey was originally placed in both Annex I and II as a member of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) group of largely high-income countries. However, it argued that its economic circumstances and historically low levels of emissions warranted differentiated treatment from other OECD members.

In 2001, it secured a unique compromise, and became the only country in the world to be removed from Annex II while staying in Annex I, with other countries formally recognising its “special circumstances”.

This left Turkey in a diplomatic limbo. It was no longer obliged to provide climate finance for developing countries, but its Annex I status meant it could not access some of the international funding available to them. The dispute over its eligibility for this support continued for years and was one factor that delayed Turkey’s ratification of the Paris agreement until 2021.

Since then, Turkey has secured substantial international support for its energy transition. Most notably, it secured a US$3.2 billion (£2.4 billion) financing package from the World Bank, France, Germany and the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development. This is funding renewable energy and energy efficiency, alongside efforts to secure private investment.

However, access to finance is only part of the problem. A round table of UN-affiliated staff and academic experts held in July 2026 found that Turkey’s national climate commitments tend to articulate ambition without specifying how exactly this will be achieved. Successful pilots rarely turn into actual policy. Likewise, the report from the round table calls for Cop31 to be an “implementation Cop” that prioritised delivering on existing commitments over announcing new ones.

Despite rapid growth in renewable energy capacity, Turkey remains heavily dependent on fossil fuels to generate electricity. Coal accounted for 33% of the country’s electricity generation in 2025, while natural gas supplied another 22%. This means phasing out coal will require a sustained strategic effort.

Turkey adopted its first climate law in 2025, which codified an ambitious target for net-zero emissions by 2053. In this context, prioritising the rhetoric of electrification at Cop31 over phasing out coal might reveal a serious limitation of Turkey’s commitment to its climate goals.

This contradiction is also apparent in Turkey’s recent deals to expand its exploration for natural gas and oil, despite its net-zero target. In early 2026, state-owned Turkish Petroleum signed agreements with fossil fuel multinationals ExxonMobil, Chevron and BP to explore and develop further oil and gasfields.

Activists have also criticised the appointment of major conglomerates linked to environmental disputes as official summit sponsors. Cop31’s “sustainable transformation partner” is a firm that plans to build more coal power plants, while another sponsor is linked to widespread deforestation to make way for coal mines.

There are also worries about how inclusive the summit will prove to be. Speakers in the host-managed Green Zone have been required to sign a declaration pledging compliance with Turkish law and “public morality”, omitting standard UN protections against discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity. The declaration also warned delegates against “interfering in internal affairs”, which could result in the silencing of political dissent.

Turkey’s unusual position in the international climate system explains some of the difficulties it has faced in its transition. But it cannot explain away the country’s continuing dependence on coal and gas, its pursuit of new fossil fuel projects or the questions surrounding the inclusiveness of the summit itself. With Australia leading the negotiations and Turkey hosting the event, Cop31 highlights these contradictions.

articles.title: States like Samoa face brutal 2027 storm season – every dollar of ‘climate cash’ counts for small islands
articles.author: Emily Wilkinson, Principal Research Fellow, Global Risks and Resilience, ODI Global
paras: Every nation is grappling with climate change, but a super El Niño is about to collide with the 2026-27 South Pacific cyclone season. This presents one of the toughest challenges yet for the world’s small island nations.

Samoa is on high alert. These islands have had a turbulent recent history with drought, heat and cyclones. In the 1980s, the El Niño cycle (when certain parts of the Pacific are warmer than usual) caused severe drought and acute water shortages, plus a heightened risk of tropical cyclones. In Samoa, families still recall the unbearable heat that withered once-lush green forests into tinder-dry matchsticks, sparking fires across the villages of Asau and Aopo.

As Samoans contend with the complex effects of El Niño in the coming months, they’ll also be experiencing the everyday consequences of climate change: 70% of the population and infrastructure are located in low-lying coastal areas. Sea levels have risen by as much as 31cm over the last three decades. This puts islanders at greater risk from flooding, more frequent and severe cyclones and saltwater intrusion (whereby dense, saline seawater infiltrates freshwater) damaging their crops.

In talanoa (story‑based dialogue, common in the Pacific) with family in Vaisala, Utusamia Barbara Carter told one of us (George Carter) how “today, the challenge is different but no less alarming. The sea is slowly rising, and our homeland is gradually being swallowed by the ocean”.

Perversely, in the short term, El Niño can lead to both high and low sea levels. During the cycle extremely low sea levels (referred to in Samoa as taimasa) can expose shallow reefs, which cause coral to die off, while the long-term trend of sea-level rise is caused by climate change.
Samoan traditions and identity are deeply tied to the land, ocean, sky and people (kinship). They and other Pacific Islanders want to stay put and maintain their way of life.

Samoa is one of 39 island nations known as small island developing states, a group that is recognised by the UN as being exceptionally vulnerable to climate change. What is new is the scale and intensity of the risk, given the compounding effects of climate change, which are occurring at a time when international cooperation on climate action is fraying.

Small island developing states continue to struggle to access adequate levels of funding to boost their climate resilience and adapt their infrastructure. The implementation of this climate finance involves long delays and red tape. Many of them feel that the world’s powers are increasingly treating them as a marginal concern, compared to more pressing issues of economic prosperity, peace and global security.
This is a big mistake. The resilience of small island developing states is increasingly bound up with all three of these issues.

These nations are spread out across the Caribbean, Pacific, Atlantic and Indian Ocean and South China Sea. They make up less than 0.5% of the world’s total land mass and less than 1% of the global population. Individually, they have little economic or military power.
These island nations may be small in landmass and population, but they govern vast ocean territories; and many sit at the centre of intensifying geopolitical competition.

Small island developing states represent 38 out of a total of 193 UN member states so they account for around 20% of votes at the UN. They have repeatedly exercised influence far beyond their economic weight. The 1.5°C temperature goal at the heart of the UN’s Paris climate agreement might never have been secured without sustained pressure from the Alliance of Small Island States, the negotiating bloc representing these island nations.

Similarly, the landmark judgment on climate change and state responsibility by the International Court for Justice in July 2025 was spearheaded by the Pacific island nation of Vanuatu. Small island developing states are, by and large, among the most successful post-colonial democracies, and their regions remain largely peaceful.

The vast ocean spaces that small island nations oversee are known as exclusive economic zones. Within these zones, countries govern everything from fishing to deep-sea mining. The exclusive economic zones that small island developing states govern span 30% of the world’s oceans. On average, that is 28 times their combined landmass. These waters encompass precious marine ecosystems like seagrasses and coral reefs that regulate the climate, support fisheries and absorb carbon.

Even with their vulnerability to extreme weather many small island developing states have built successful economies with high levels of per capita income since independence. Entrepreneurs in small island developing states are producing green technologies and digital services with applications beyond their domestic economies.
Australia plans to use its presidency of the UN climate summit Cop31 to highlight the special circumstances of small island developing states, but it must also achieve some tangible results.

One big step forward would be to improve access to existing flows of already pledged climate cash that isn’t reaching the right places fast enough. Island states need low-interest loans and grants, known as concessional finance, so they can invest in their own resilience without getting deeper into debt.

The new Pacific Resilience Facility is a climate finance mechanism owned and led by Pacific people that launched earlier this year. It is a good example of how wealthier countries might help islands like Samoa prepare for the new reality.

Wealthy nations could also recognise specific small island vulnerabilities by ensuring there is a “climate exception”. Small island nations whose income levels mean they are no longer eligible for official development assistance, could be made eligible again but just for assistance that is for building climate resilience. This would mean that highly vulnerable small islands with higher incomes don’t get shut out of aid budgets that will be essential to their survival in years to come.
Emily Wilkinson receives funding from the UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office and the Government of Ireland's Department for Foreign Affairs and Trade.
George Carter receives funding from Australian Department of Foreign Affairs, and Secretariat of the Pacific Regional Environment Program.

articles.title: Andy Burnham and climate change: where does the prime minister really stand?
articles.author: James Jackson, Lecturer and Research Fellow, School of Social Sciences, University of Manchester
paras: Since becoming prime minister, Andy Burnham has set out a relatively ambitious political agenda. He has outlined plans for a national care service, a “Great British Grid” and suggested a rethink of the UK’s relationship with the European Union.
But one big omission of Burnham’s agenda is climate policy. Amid the proposals that put clear water between him and his predecessor Keir Starmer, Burnham’s climate agenda remains unknown.

The prime minister has reiterated his intention to reach net zero by 2050 (though this target is contentious due to whether it actually reflects climate science as well as the extent to which it depends upon as yet unavailable technology). He has also pledged to attend Cop31, the UN climate summit currently underway in Turkey, in person. However, the budget – Burnham’s first real opportunity to set out his vision – raised concerns about whether his political rhetoric could translate into a coherent climate policy.

The budget revealed that increased defence spending would come at the cost of £3 billion of cuts at the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero. Subsidies for heat pumps, boilers, the warm homes plan, hydrogen and carbon capture and storage were the most prominent policies to be culled. This not only limits the UK’s green industrial policy, but suggests that energy security is still not considered to be part of national security.
Energy security and rising bills

For years, the UK has been misaligned with its own carbon budgets set under the Climate Change Act 2008. After the Conservatives began to question the objective of net zero towards the end of their term in office, the election of the first Labour government in 14 years was expected to mark a turning point.

Burnham’s climate position has become entwined (and somewhat undermined) by energy security concerns following the so-called fossilflationary pressures caused by the the US and Israel’s conflict with Iran. This has fed into the licensing of the Jackdaw gasfield 150 miles east of Aberdeen. This is part of Burnham’s self-described “pragmatic” approach to new drilling in the North Sea.

The initial justification was that the move would improve energy security by increasing the domestic supply of oil and gas. But critics say that increasing supply has little to no effect on domestic bills, as prices are set by international markets. Revenues made from the project will be used to finance an Energy Wealth Fund to invest in green technologies elsewhere.

Then there’s the cost of living. As winter approaches, an increasing number of households will have to choose between heating and eating. In response, Chancellor John Healey’s budget removed green levies from consumer bills. These levies fund environmental programmes such as renewable schemes, but the money will now be sourced from general taxation.
This does reduce bills in the short term. But the shift, combined with other cuts, raises doubts over the long term.

It’s argued that removing green levies from bills will reduce the relative cost of energy. This is a salient argument as the UK approaches a period of higher energy demand to heat the country’s homes. But critics say that reducing support for green energy infrastructure will delay the advent of abundant cheap energy.
Political and economic tests

Labour now has two challenges. The first is the political bind the party finds itself in. Its manifesto does not contain anything resembling an ambitious climate policy. Although Burnham represents a change at the top, he has not won the right to depart from the platform upon which Starmer was elected.
Whether this represents a constraint on Burnham’s political vision or just more of the same on a limited climate policy is up for debate.

The second is an economic bind due to the UK’s tight fiscal position. This is despite taxation being at a historically high level – much of which has come from “fiscal drag” as taxpayers are pulled into higher tax bands.

The broader issues are that ten-year UK gilt yields – the rate the government pays on its debt – have risen to 5.13%. The irony of the rise in gilt yields is that they have increased primarily because of “fossilflation” as supply-side shocks have fed into energy prices.
As a result, the Bank of England has raised interest rates for the first time in three years, to 4%. This will further increase borrowing costs and make life less affordable for UK households.

And yet Labour’s propositions only put its climate policy into further doubt. It remains to be seen whether it will grant a licence for the Rosebank oil field, west of Shetland, which is larger than Jackdaw. Unless the government bends to political pressure, Burnham and energy secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh could make the same arguments about energy security again.

In the meantime, Burnham has signalled his desire to raise tariffs on Chinese green technology to align the UK more closely to the EU. This would be a bid to answer security worries, but tariffs on the cheapest and largest source of green technology places climate second to geopolitical concerns.
Under Burnham, climate policy has, at best, been lost amid the prime minister’s broader political platform. At worst, he has concluded it is a price worth paying to achieve his other objectives.
